newsitem.title: UK: RISING CONSUMER CONFIDENCE TO FUEL RESTAURANT BOOM - CONSULTANCY.
newsitem.headline: RISING CONSUMER CONFIDENCE TO FUEL RESTAURANT BOOM - CONSULTANCY.

text.p: Rising consumer confidence and a bit of extra household cash is expected to fuel a boom in Britain's restaurant business this year, a consultancy said on Monday.

Retail Directions, a UK retail consultancy, said a "major boom in eating out during 1997" would be sparked partly by the flotation of building societies which will hand back cash to millions of individual building society members.

"The growth in consumer confidence combined with funds from building society flotations will filter into the leisure markets and result in an appreciable increase in restaurant and pub food business," it said.
One of the flotations, by Halifax Building Society, this summer will be the biggest ever on the London Stock Exchange.
The flotations will convert the building societies -- which are mortgage lenders and savings institutions owned by their borrowing and saving members -- into public companies.

"The money coming from the building society flotations during 1997 will be spent by the family on leisure pursuits and not on household items or improvements as has always happened in the past," Robert Eldridge, Retail Directions managing director, said in a statement.

Retail Directions also predicted that shoppers' enthusiasm for "loyalty cards" issued by British supermarket retail groups will rapidly diminish in 1997 unless real benefits were perceived by consumers.
Britain's major supermarket groups have all launched loyalty cards in the last few years that offer shoppers things like cash rebates, points towards other purchases and air travel miles.
The loyalty cards are one of the main tools being used by the food retail groups to compete against one another.

"The rewards offered by retailers will have to become more exciting and more tangible, otherwise customers will become disillusioned, disappointed and dejected," Conrad Rowland, Retail Directions director, said.
"The loyalty card is in danger of becoming the marketing tool of 1997 that retailers could live to regret," he said.
